name: Ecdysterone
lead: Ecdysterone, more formally 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), is a naturally occurring ecdysteroid hormone that controls molting and metamorphosis in insects and crustaceans; it is also produced by plants such as Cyanotis vaga, Ajuga turkestanica and Rhaponticum carthamoides, where it is thought to defend against herbivores [1]. Spinach and quinoa are listed among dietary sources [3].

Mammals lack the arthropod ecdysone receptor, but ecdysterone still affects mammalian systems, and in mammals it is hypothesised to bind estrogen receptor beta (ERbeta) [1][12]. It is sold as a supplement for bodybuilding and sport and is also being developed as an investigational compound for muscle-related conditions [1][13].

Research on its anabolic effects in people is limited. A 2006 study concluded that a modest oral amount did not significantly affect training adaptations, while a 2019 controlled study funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) reported larger increases in muscle mass and bench press performance with ecdysterone than without [1][7]. Replication evidence is sparse.
infobox: Insects and crustaceans; Cyanotis vaga, Ajuga turkestanica, Rhaponticum carthamoides, spinach [1][3]

paras: Ecdysterone is marketed in bodybuilding supplements. T Nation members describe adding it to pre-workouts and stacks alongside ashwagandha, tongkat ali, fadogia, laxogenin and turkesterone [14][15][16][17], and some report that it made a 'noteworthy difference' in strength, recovery, body fat and well-being in combination with other products [14]. A 2021 poster recommends only 'proper products with standardized contents' [18]. Another suggests it as a way to lower estrogen effects instead of raising testosterone, warning of underdosed supplements [19].

In 2001 a T Nation thread proposed a forum experiment to test ecdysterone, asking supporters to supply numbers [20]. In 2007 a user described smoking a suma root powder containing 2 percent ecdysterone as an experiment [21].

Registered trials include 20E in sarcopenia (NCT03452488), in prediabetes (NCT03906201), in giardiasis (NCT04827537), and in patients with obesity starting semaglutide to assess muscle wasting (NCT07411378) [22][23][24][25]. Wikipedia notes the FDA approved a study of 20E in obesity in 2024 [1].

A 2006 study found that 30 mg per day orally did not significantly change anabolic or catabolic responses, body composition or training adaptations [1]. A 2019 controlled clinical trial in Archives of Toxicology, funded by WADA, reported significantly greater increases in muscle mass and one-repetition bench press in participants given ecdysterone, with a dose-responsive effect [1][7]. A 2025 12-week randomised double-blind training study tested a commercial phytosteroid product containing 20E and diosgenin and examined the reliability of its labelling [8]. A 2024 review covers ecdysterone and turkesterone in sport [3].

Grokipedia summarises human trials as mixed and attributes some null results to commercial supplements containing far less 20E than labelled [2]; this is from an AI-generated source and was not independently verified.

Long-term human safety has not been established in the sources cited. Grokipedia describes animal data as showing low toxicity [2]. Forum users caution about underdosed supplements and recommend standardised products [18][19].

In arthropods 20E acts through the ecdysone receptor [1]. In mammals, a 2014 study reported that estrogen receptor beta is involved in skeletal muscle hypertrophy induced by ecdysterone [12], and the WADA-funded human study's abstract states that the anabolic effect is thought to be mediated by estrogen receptor binding [7]. Wikipedia describes relatively selective activation of ERbeta in human muscle cells [1]. Grokipedia adds activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways [2].
Research on other effects includes bone regeneration via BMP-2/SMAD/RUNX2 signalling and protection of rat liver mitochondria under immobilisation stress, both preclinical [9][10].

Wikipedia notes high oral bioavailability in animals [1]. Studies have examined urinary excretion of ecdysterone and its metabolites after spinach consumption and possible dietary sources of ecdysterone in urine, relevant to anti-doping interpretation [4][5].

Ecdysteroid research began with insect hormones; Grokipedia states 20E was first isolated from the silk moth in the 1960s [2]. Studies in Drosophila in the 1970s and 1980s used ecdysterone to study gene induction and heat-shock responses [11]. Wikipedia describes use of ecdysteroids as inducers in transgenic animals as a research tool [1]. In supplement culture, a 2001 T Nation thread already debated whether ecdysterone 'works' [20].

Human trials of ecdysterone for muscle: a 2006 study [1], the 2019 WADA-funded study [7], and the 2025 12-week trial of a 20E and diosgenin product [8]. Reviews: ecdysterone and turkesterone in sport and nutrition [3] and degenerative diseases [6].
Registered trials listed above cover sarcopenia, prediabetes, giardiasis and obesity with semaglutide [22][23][24][25].

timeline.event: Ecdysteroid hormones are identified in insects; Grokipedia dates 20E isolation from silk moth to the 1960s [2].
A study of oral 20E finds no significant effect on training adaptations [1].
Study links estrogen receptor beta to ecdysterone-induced muscle hypertrophy [12].
WADA-funded study reports greater muscle mass and bench press gains with ecdysterone [7].
12-week study of a commercial 20E and diosgenin product examines labelling reliability [8].

lore.intro: On T Nation ecdysterone has been a subject of debate since the early 2000s and is now typically mentioned as an add-on supplement, with repeated cautions about product quality [20][18][19].

claims.claim: Ecdysterone is an anabolic that rivals prohibited steroids
claims.believers: Posters cite it as a strength and hypertrophy aid and report personal improvements in strength and recovery; a user on 'some Russian ecdysterone' says it does appear to work [14][26].
claims.experts: A WADA-funded 2019 study reported dose-dependent gains in muscle mass and bench press; a 2006 study found no significant effect; the evidence base is small [1][7].

claims.claim: It works through estrogen receptor beta, not androgen receptors
claims.believers: A forum poster calls it an estrogen beta receptor agonist and says it may provide strength through a different pathway [18].
claims.experts: A 2014 study reported ERbeta involvement in ecdysterone-induced muscle hypertrophy [12]; Wikipedia says it is hypothesised to bind ERbeta [1].

claims.claim: Product quality matters: many supplements are underdosed
claims.believers: Posters advise buying only standardised products and warn of underdosed supplements [18][19].
claims.experts: A 2025 trial examined the reliability of the labelling of a commercial phytosteroid product [8]; Grokipedia states some products contain far less than labelled [2].

claims.claim: Ecdysterone is a way to improve hormone balance without raising testosterone
claims.believers: A poster suggests focusing on lowering estrogen via ecdysterone rather than raising testosterone [19].
claims.experts: No study cited here measured estrogen levels with ecdysterone supplementation.

claims.claim: Ecdysterone can be smoked to bypass the stomach
claims.believers: A 2007 user tried smoking a root powder containing ecdysterone expecting direct absorption [21].
claims.experts: No study cited here has tested this route; Wikipedia notes oral bioavailability in animals is high [1].
